Intersection homology (IH∗pˉ​​(X))

Words: 566 Articles: 11
Algebraic topology OurBigBook.com
Intersection homology is the homology of a chain complex in which chains and their boundaries satisfy codimension-dependent perversity restrictions at singular strata. Unless specified otherwise coefficients here are Q. Ordinary homology is recovered on manifolds.

Perversity (pˉ​)

Words: 150 Articles: 4
Intersection homology OurBigBook.com
A traditional perversity is a function pˉ​:{2,3,…}→Z satisfying pˉ​(2)=0 and pˉ​(k+1)−pˉ​(k)∈{0,1}. It specifies how far chains may meet strata of codimension k.

Allowable singular simplex

Words: 81 Articles: 1
Perversity OurBigBook.com
An i-dimensional singular simplex σ:Δi→X is pˉ​-allowable if σ−1(XN−k​) is contained in the (i−k+pˉ​(k))-skeleton of Δi for every k≥2. A negative skeleton is empty. Individual faces need not be allowable; this is why the definition of intersection chains separately imposes allowability on the total boundary.
Intersection chains (IS∗pˉ​​(X))
Words: 33
Allowable singular simplex OurBigBook.com
The group ISipˉ​​(X) consists of finite singular chains whose nonzero simplices are allowable singular simplices and whose boundary, after cancellation, also consists of allowable simplices. Since ∂2=0, these groups form a chain complex. Its homology is intersection homology.

Upper middle perversity (nˉ(k)=⌈(k−2)/2⌉)

Words: 19
Perversity OurBigBook.com
The upper middle perversity is nˉ(k)=⌈(k−2)/2⌉. It differs from the lower middle perversity by one at odd codimensions, and is complementary to it.

Lower middle perversity (mˉ(k)=⌊(k−2)/2⌋)

Words: 21
Perversity OurBigBook.com
The lower middle perversity is mˉ(k)=⌊(k−2)/2⌋. The complementary upper middle perversity is nˉ(k)=⌈(k−2)/2⌉, and mˉ(k)+nˉ(k)=k−2. They agree at even codimensions.

Intersection homology cone formula

Words: 127 Articles: 1
Intersection homology OurBigBook.com
For a compact (N−1)-dimensional link L and traditional perversity pˉ​, finite-chain intersection homology of its open cone is IHipˉ​​(cL)=IHipˉ​​(L) for i<N−1−pˉ​(N) and zero for i≥N−1−pˉ​(N). Below the cutoff both chains and possible filling chains avoid the vertex. At and above the cutoff the cone on any allowable cycle is an allowable filling: its new vertex is allowed precisely when 0≤i+1−N+pˉ​(N).

Intersection homology of an even-dimensional suspension

Words: 57
Intersection homology cone formula OurBigBook.com
For dimL=2n−1 and lower middle perversity, the suspension with two distinct vertices has IHi​(SuspL)=IHi​(L) for i<n, zero for i=n, and IHi−1​(L) for i>n. Cover it by its two open cones. The Mayer–Vietoris sequence compares their truncated groups with IH∗​(L); below n the overlap map is the injective signed diagonal, and above n both cone groups vanish.

Intersection cohomology (IHpˉ​i​(X))

Words: 257 Articles: 3
Intersection homology OurBigBook.com
In the Deligne-sheaf convention, IHpˉ​i​(X)=Hi(X,ICpˉ​​), with ICpˉ​​ normalized in degree zero on the regular stratum. For a compact oriented N-dimensional pseudomanifold over a field, IHpˉ​i​(X)≅IHN−ipˉ​​(X) and it is dual to IHiqˉ​​(X), where pˉ​(k)+qˉ​(k)=k−2. Thus the dual of lower-middle singular chains uses the upper-middle Deligne sheaf. The two middle conventions agree on Witt spaces.

Capped-boundary intersection cohomology

Words: 73
Intersection cohomology OurBigBook.com
Let a compact oriented (2m+1)-manifold M have collared boundary B, and cap B by its closed cone. In the lower-middle Deligne convention the result has IHi=Hi(M) for i<m, IHm=im(Hm(M,B)→Hm(M)), and IHi=Hi(M,B) for i>m. Excision identifies the relative intersection groups with H∗(M,B); the cone neighbourhood has Hi(B) only for i<m, so its long exact sequence gives the formula. The cap is Witt exactly when Hm(B;Q)=0.

Intersection complex (ICpˉ​​)

Words: 120 Articles: 1
Intersection cohomology OurBigBook.com
The degree-zero normalized Deligne intersection complex extends the constant sheaf from the regular stratum by successive derived direct images and cohomological truncations at degree pˉ​(k) when codimension-k strata are added. Its hypercohomology defines intersection cohomology. On a cone with vertex of codimension k, its local cohomology is the link intersection cohomology in degrees at most pˉ​(k) and zero above.
Intersection-complex support and cosupport axioms
Words: 65
Intersection complex OurBigBook.com
For an isolated singular point of an N-dimensional oriented pseudomanifold, the unshifted middle intersection complex restricts to Q on the regular stratum and has no negative cohomology. Its support condition is Hj(ix∗​ICpˉ​​)=0 for j>pˉ​(N); its cosupport condition is Hj(ix!​ICpˉ​​)=0 for j≤pˉ​(N)+1. These conditions, together with constructibility and normalization, characterize it. On a Witt space they are exchanged by IC≅D(IC)[−N].

Homotopy colimit of spaces

Words: 46
Algebraic topology OurBigBook.com
A homotopy colimit of spaces is the homotopy-invariant replacement for a colimit of spaces. For a filtered diagram of CW complexes with subcomplex inclusions, the union is a model: the inclusions are cofibrations, and every sphere map and homotopy has image in a finite subcomplex. A suspension spectrum carries this construction to the corresponding homotopy colimit of spectra.

Stable homotopy theory

Words: 1k Articles: 36
Algebraic topology OurBigBook.com
Stable homotopy theory studies topological spectra, which retain the information that persists under repeated reduced suspension. Its stable homotopy category admits invertible suspension of spectra and exact cofiber sequences of spectra.

Universe for spectra

Words: 76 Articles: 1
Stable homotopy theory OurBigBook.com
A universe for spectra is a countably infinite-dimensional real inner product space, normally with its direct-limit topology, used to index finite-dimensional suspension coordinates. A cofinal indexing family contains arbitrarily large finite-dimensional subspaces.

Subordinate flag for a family of linear isometries

Words: 49
Universe for spectra OurBigBook.com
Given a compact parameter space X and a family fx​:U→U′ of linear isometries, a subordinate flag for a family of linear isometries consists of nested cofinal source and target subspaces Vi​,Wi​ with fx​(Vi​)⊂Wi​ for every x. After enlarging the target stages, compactness makes this possible for every finite source stage. It permits simultaneous finite-dimensional Thom space constructions.

Homotopy colimit of spectra (hocolimTj​)

Words: 75 Articles: 1
Stable homotopy theory OurBigBook.com
A homotopy colimit of spectra is the derived colimit of a diagram of topological spectra. For a sequential diagram T0​→T1​→⋯, it is the cofiber of spectra of 1−s:⋁j​Tj​→⋁j​Tj​, where s uses the bonding maps into the next summands.

Milnor exact sequence for maps of spectra

Words: 43
Homotopy colimit of spectra OurBigBook.com
For D=hocolimj​Tj​, applying [−,E]st​ to the telescope cofiber sequence of spectra gives
0⟶limj1​[ΣTj​,E]st​⟶[D,E]st​⟶limj​[Tj​,E]st​⟶0.
(1)
Here lim1 is the cokernel of 1−r on the product of the inverse tower, where r uses its bonding maps. This records the obstruction to uniqueness when compatible stage maps are realized.

Cofiber of spectra (cofib(u))

Words: 57 Articles: 1
Stable homotopy theory OurBigBook.com
The homotopy cofiber of spectra of u:A→B is the derived pushout B∪A​CA. It fits into a cofiber sequence of spectra.

Cofiber sequence of spectra

Words: 40
Cofiber of spectra OurBigBook.com
A cofiber sequence of spectra A→B→C→ΣA induces exact sequences after either mapping into or out of a fixed topological spectrum, and on stable homotopy groups. In particular the second map is zero precisely when the first map admits a right inverse in the stable homotopy category.

Smash product of spectra (D∧E)

Words: 107 Articles: 2
Stable homotopy theory OurBigBook.com
The derived smash product of spectra is the symmetric monoidal product on the stable homotopy category. It has unit sphere spectrum, preserves cofiber sequences of spectra and homotopy colimits of spectra in each variable, and satisfies Σ∞X∧Σ∞Y≃Σ∞(X∧Y).

Function spectrum (F(A,E))

Words: 81 Articles: 1
Smash product of spectra OurBigBook.com
The internal function spectrum is characterized by [C,F(A,E)]st​=[C∧A,E]st​. For a based space K, notation F(K,E) abbreviates F(Σ∞K,E).
Function spectrum with values in a ring spectrum
Words: 63
Function spectrum OurBigBook.com
If E is a ring spectrum, then F(X+​,E) is a ring spectrum. Its multiplication is adjoint to evaluating the two functions on the two copies supplied by the diagonal of X, then multiplying in E. Its unit is the constant unit function. Coassociativity of the diagonal and associativity in E prove the associative identity; the counit and unit identities prove both unit laws.

Stable homotopy category ([D,E]st​)

Words: 33 Articles: 1
Stable homotopy theory OurBigBook.com
The stable homotopy category is obtained from topological spectra by inverting stable equivalences of spectra. Its morphisms are abelian groups; for a cellular source and fibrant target they are spectrum homotopy classes of point-set maps of topological spectra.

A map of topological spectra inducing isomorphisms on every stable homotopy group is a stable equivalence of spectra.

Spectrum (topology) OurBigBook.com
A connective spectrum has πq​E=0 for q<0. This makes the homological Atiyah-Hirzebruch spectral sequence first quadrant for a based space, and prevents negative coefficient degrees from affecting its first nonzero represented homology theory.

Words: 109 Articles: 1
Connective spectrum OurBigBook.com
If E is connective spectrum in the sense of a connective spectrum, π0​E≅Z, and X is (n−1)-connected with n≥2, then En​(X)≅πn​(X). In the homological Atiyah-Hirzebruch spectral sequence, the only nonzero term in total degree n is Hn​(X;π0​E). Incoming differentials have negative coefficient degree, and outgoing differentials have spatial degree below n. The Hurewicz theorem identifies this term with πn​X.
Connective generalized homology detects simply connected equivalences
Words: 48
Bottom-degree generalized Hurewicz isomorphism OurBigBook.com
For a connective spectrum with π0​E≅Z, an E-homology isomorphism of simply connected spaces is a weak homotopy equivalence. Its simply connected homotopy mapping cone is E-acyclic. If it had a first nonzero integral homology group, the Hurewicz theorem and the bottom-degree generalized Hurewicz isomorphism would produce a nonzero E-homology group. Thus the cone is integrally acyclic and the homological Whitehead theorem applies.

A ring spectrum is a unital associative monoid object of the stable homotopy category under the smash product of spectra. It has μ:E∧E→E and η:S→E, satisfying the associative and two unit identities. Structured ring spectra additionally specify coherent point-set or higher homotopies; a ring object alone does not assert those enhancements.

Lusternik–Schnirelmann category (cat(X))

Words: 170 Articles: 1
Algebraic topology OurBigBook.com
Use the unnormalized convention: the least number of open subsets covering X whose inclusions into X are null-homotopic. The subsets need not themselves be contractible. This number is one for a nonempty contractible space. If r positive-degree classes have nonzero product, a cover by r categorical sets would make that product zero by relative cup products; hence cat(X)≥r+1.

Lusternik–Schnirelmann critical point theorem

Words: 111
Lusternik–Schnirelmann category OurBigBook.com
Every smooth real-valued function on a closed connected smooth manifold has at least its unnormalized Lusternik–Schnirelmann category many distinct critical points. No nondegeneracy hypothesis is required. If there are infinitely many critical points the bound is immediate; in the finite case, the sublevel-set deformation argument shows that category can increase only at critical levels, by at most the number of critical points on that level. In conjunction with cup length, this gives at least r+1 critical points whenever there is a nonzero r-fold positive-degree cup product. This theorem is distinct from the antipodal covering theorem also sometimes named the Lusternik–Schnirelmann theorem. A primary account of the critical-point formulation is Conley pairs in geometry—Lusternik–Schnirelmann theory and more.

Every continuous map f:Sn→Rn takes the same value at some antipodal pair. Equivalently, every continuous antipodal map Sn→Rn has a zero, and there is no antipodal map Sn→Sn−1.

A cover of Sd by d+1 closed sets has a member containing an antipodal pair. The equivalent version for open sets follows by shrinking finite open covers on a compact metric space; the reverse implication follows by enlarging antipodal-pair-free closed sets slightly. This is a covering formulation of the Borsuk-Ulam theorem.

Antipodal-free closed cover from simplex Voronoi cells (Ci​={x∈Sn:x⋅vi​≥x⋅vj​ for all j})

Words: 87
Lusternik–Schnirelmann theorem OurBigBook.com
Let v0​,…,vn+1​ be the vertices of a regular simplex centered at zero in Rn+1. The displayed spherical Voronoi cells are a closed cover by n+2 sets. If x and −x belonged to the same cell, all their scalar products with the vertices would coincide. Their sum is zero and the vertices span the ambient vector space, so this would force x=0, a contradiction. Thus each cell contains no antipodal pair. Together with the Lusternik-Schnirelmann-Borsuk theorem, this shows n+2 is the minimum number of antipodal-free members of a finite closed cover.

Such a partition of unity comes from normalizing the distance to a set functions d(x,Sd∖Ui​). The Borsuk-Ulam theorem applied to (ϕ1​,…,ϕd​) gives equal values at an antipodal pair. The sum condition makes ϕ0​ equal too, and some common positive value places both points in one Ui​.

CW complex

Words: 2k Articles: 29
Algebraic topology OurBigBook.com
A CW complex is built inductively by attaching discs along maps from their boundary spheres. Its n-skeleton contains all cells of dimension at most n.

Compact subsets of CW complexes lie in finite subcomplexes

Words: 88
CW complex OurBigBook.com
A compact subset of a CW complex is contained in a finite CW complex that is a subcomplex of the original complex. Otherwise choose one point in each of infinitely many cells met by the subset. The closure-finiteness axiom makes each closed cell meet the chosen set in finitely many points. The weak topology axiom then makes the chosen set, and each of its subsets, closed. It is consequently an infinite closed discrete subspace of the compact subset, a contradiction. Only finitely many cells are met; their closures form a finite subcomplex containing the subset.

CW complex OurBigBook.com
The q-skeleton of a CW complex is the subcomplex consisting of its topological cells of dimension at most q. A cellular map preserves these skeleta. The cellular approximation theorem lets continuous maps respect this filtration up to homotopy.

Topological cell (eq)

CW complex OurBigBook.com
An open q-cell of a CW complex is a copy of an open q-dimensional ball. Its characteristic map is a map from a closed ball whose interior parametrizes that cell and whose boundary lands in the preceding skeleton. The characteristic map need not be injective on the boundary. Each oriented cell gives one generator of the cellular chain complex.

A CW pair consists of a CW complex X and a subcomplex A. Its inclusion is a cofibration, so homotopies on A extend across X. The relative lifting property of a Serre fibration for such pairs allows specified boundary lifts to be retained while lifting a homotopy.

CW complex OurBigBook.com
Attaching a q-cell along ϕ:Sq−1→X forms the quotient of X⊔Dq identifying each boundary point with its image under ϕ. A constant attaching map gives X∨Sq. An attaching map can affect the cohomology ring even when it does not change the additive cohomology groups.

Homotopy-group effect of attaching higher cells (πi​(X∪α​ei+1)=πi​(X)/⟨π1​(X)⋅[α]⟩(i≥2))

Words: 92
Cell attachment OurBigBook.com
Attaching cells of dimension i+1 to a connected CW complex, for i≥2, preserves all homotopy groups below degree i. In degree i it takes the quotient by the subgroup generated by the attaching maps and their translates under the fundamental group action. This follows from the relative homotopy sequence and the generation of the first nonzero relative group by the new cells. In particular, a single attaching map representing a generator of πi​≅Z kills that group even when the fundamental group is nontrivial. Higher attachments can create higher homotopy groups, which may then be killed at later stages.

Weak topology of a CW complex

Words: 82
CW complex OurBigBook.com
The weak topology of a CW complex is determined by its closed cells: a subset is closed if and only if its inverse image under every characteristic map from a closed cell is closed. A map out of the complex is continuous when its restrictions along those characteristic maps are continuous. This is distinct from the weak topology of a vector space. Taking the product with a locally finite CW complex, such as a closed interval with its finite cell structure, retains the corresponding CW weak topology.

Graph (topology)

Words: 45
CW complex OurBigBook.com
A topological graph is a CW complex with only zero-cells and one-cells, called vertices and edges. Edge endpoints attach to vertices; loops, multiple edges and infinitely many edges are allowed. A subgraph in this setting is a CW subcomplex. A connected acyclic graph is a tree and is a contractible space.

CW subcomplex

Words: 47
CW complex OurBigBook.com
A CW subcomplex is a union of cells of a CW complex containing the attaching boundary of every included cell. In a combinatorial 2-complex, including a two-cell therefore includes every edge in its boundary. A connected CW subcomplex has a connected 1-skeleton, whose intrinsic path metric may differ from the ambient graph metric.

Words: 42
CW complex OurBigBook.com
The one-skeleton X(1) of a CW complex is the union of its zero-cells and one-cells. It is a graph. The unit-edge path metric measures the infimum of lengths of paths in this graph; it is different from metrics that allow paths through two-cell interiors.

2-complex

Words: 411 Articles: 6
CW complex OurBigBook.com
A two-dimensional CW complex has cells only in dimensions zero, one and two. In a combinatorial two-complex the two-cells are polygons attached by combinatorial edge paths. Its 1-skeleton carries the path metric assigning length one to each edge. Compact combinatorial complexes have finitely many cells, so their cell-boundary lengths have a finite maximum.

Disc diagram

Words: 361 Articles: 5
2-complex OurBigBook.com
A disc diagram over a combinatorial 2-complex is a finite contractible planar combinatorial complex together with a combinatorial map to that complex. Its exterior boundary circuit records a null-homotopic path. Tree portions and cut vertices are allowed; the diagram need not be an embedded disk or map injectively. Its area is its number of two-cells.
Disc diagram ladder
Words: 75
Disc diagram OurBigBook.com
A ladder is a disc diagram whose blocks form a linear chain, each block a two-cell or a connecting edge, with cells attached successively along interior arcs. Its boundary consists of two opposite side paths between its ends. Every cell meets both side paths. If cell perimeters are bounded by L, each point of one side is within L/2 of the other by traveling around a cell boundary; connecting edge paths coincide on the two sides.

Words: 61
Disc diagram OurBigBook.com
A spur is an exposed degree-one vertex and its incident edge in a disc diagram. The exterior boundary runs out along that edge and immediately back. Thus a spur in the interior of a boundary side contradicts that side being a reduced combinatorial path or a metric geodesic. A diagram with no two-cells may be a tree and have spurs rather than shells.

Disc diagram OurBigBook.com
A shell is an exposed two-cell in a disc diagram, with perimeter split as an exterior boundary arc Q and an interior path P. An i-shell has P consisting of i interior pieces. Under C′(1/6), an i-shell with i≤3 has ∣P∣<∣∂R∣/2<∣Q∣, so removal replaces a long exterior path by a strictly shorter path.

Words: 58
Disc diagram OurBigBook.com
A closed combinatorial path in a 2-complex is null-homotopic exactly when it is the boundary path of a disc diagram over that complex. A finite cellular null-homotopy can be arranged into such a planar diagram; conversely the contractible diagram supplies a null-homotopy. In a group presentation, this is the geometric form of expressing a trivial word as a product of conjugates of relators.

Disc diagram OurBigBook.com
A disc diagram is reduced if it has no adjacent pair of two-cells that can be folded together across their common boundary and removed while preserving the outside boundary. A minimum-area diagram is reduced. Among diagrams of minimum area, minimizing the number of edges removes unnecessary tree portions. Internal common arcs in a reduced diagram satisfy the applicable small cancellation theory piece bounds.

Cellular approximation theorem

Words: 170 Articles: 1
Cellular map OurBigBook.com
A continuous map between CW complexes is homotopic to a cellular map. If the map is already cellular on a subcomplex, the homotopy can be taken relative to that subcomplex. In particular, a map from a d-dimensional CW complex can be deformed into the d-skeleton of the target. This permits finite cellular chain complexes to compute induced homology maps, and turns maps to Complex projective space into maps to an appropriate finite-dimensional projective skeleton.
Dimension reduction of sphere maps into CW skeleta ([Sn,Xn]⟶[Sn,X] is surjective)
Words: 108
Cellular approximation theorem OurBigBook.com
A map from the n-sphere to a CW complex can be homotoped into its n-skeleton. By compact subsets of CW complexes lie in finite subcomplexes, its image lies in a finite subcomplex. For a top-dimensional cell of dimension d>n, use smooth approximation of maps into Euclidean space in its interior, with a cutoff supported away from the cell boundary. The Sard theorem supplies a point in a smaller interior ball omitted by the smoothed map; the cutoff is chosen so the transition region also avoids that point. Radial retraction from the omitted point pushes the image into the cell boundary and fixes all other cells. Repeating over the finitely many higher-dimensional cells proves the assertion, without assuming the initial continuous image has measure zero.

Euclidean embedding by finite cell attachment

Words: 78
Finite CW complex OurBigBook.com
Suppose a compact skeleton Y embeds as e(Y)⊂Rm. Attach a disk by a:Sk−1→Y and extend its boundary coordinate map radially by G(ru)=re(a(u)). Map the disk to (G(x),(1−∣x∣)x,1−∣x∣) and Y to (e(y),0,0). The boundary identifications agree; a positive last coordinate recovers each interior point. This defines a continuous injection of the compact quotient into Euclidean space, hence an embedding. Repeating proves Hausdorffness and Euclidean embeddability for every finite CW complex, without assuming triangulability of arbitrary attaching maps.

A homotopy between maps f,g:Y→X is a continuous map H:Y×[0,1]→X with H(y,0)=f(y) and H(y,1)=g(y).

Homotopy category

Words: 312 Articles: 5
Homotopy OurBigBook.com
The homotopy category of based CW complexes has spaces as objects and based homotopy classes as morphisms. Composition is well-defined because composition with continuous maps preserves homotopies. A based homotopy equivalence becomes an isomorphism. Rational localization instead inverts rational homotopy equivalences, producing a category represented by rational spaces. More general model categories have analogous homotopy categories obtained by inverting their weak equivalences.

For maps A→X and A→Y, the double mapping cylinder X⊔(A×I)⊔Y, with each endpoint attached by its given map, models the homotopy pushout. A map out of this model is a pair of maps on X and Y together with a homotopy between their restrictions to A. This is why compatible homotopy classes extend over a homotopy pushout. For a CW pair, the inclusion is a cofibration and the ordinary pushout gives the same homotopy type.

An H-space whose multiplication is homotopy associative and admits a homotopy inverse. These operations give [X,Y]∗​ a group structure for every based CW complex X. A loop space is the basic example: concatenate paths, use reversal for inversion, and use reparametrization for homotopy associativity. A bare H-space should not automatically be treated as a group object.

Study homotopy after killing torsion, especially for simply connected spaces of finite type. The rational Whitehead theorem detects rational homotopy equivalences by rational homology, while Sullivan minimal models encode rational homotopy generators and cohomological relations.

Words: 65
Rational homotopy theory OurBigBook.com
A connected space is nilpotent when its fundamental group is nilpotent and its action on each higher homotopy group is nilpotent: the module has a finite filtration whose successive quotients have trivial group action. Simply connected spaces satisfy these conditions automatically. They are the natural setting for localization and rationalization, since fibrewise coefficient localization is compatible with the successive untwisted stages of such a filtration.

Rational space

Words: 200 Articles: 3
Rational homotopy theory OurBigBook.com
In the simply connected homotopy category, a rational space is a simply connected CW complex whose positive homotopy groups are vector spaces over Q. Multiplication by every nonzero integer on these groups is invertible. More generally one uses nilpotent spaces with localized fundamental group and higher homotopy groups; the simply connected version avoids local-coefficient twisting.

For simply connected X, rationalization of a topological space is a map r:X→XQ​ to a rational space inducing πn​(XQ​)=πn​(X)⊗Q. It is also a rational homology equivalence. Its universal property is the bijection r∗:[XQ​,Z]→[X,Z] for every rational space Z. A Postnikov tower constructs it by replacing each fibre group with its rational tensor product and transporting the Postnikov invariant through the resulting cohomology isomorphism, then taking the homotopy inverse limit.

A map between simply connected spaces is a rational homotopy equivalence when it induces isomorphisms πn​(X)⊗Q→πn​(Y)⊗Q in every degree. Equivalently it induces an equivalence of their rationalizations, or a rational homology isomorphism by the rational Whitehead theorem. Spaces have the same rational homotopy type when they are connected by a zigzag of such maps. This is distinct from rational homotopy equivalence of algebraic cycles.

The rational homotopy type of a simply connected space is its equivalence class under zigzags of rational homotopy equivalences, or equivalently the homotopy type of its rationalization of a topological space. For the usual finite-type spaces, it is encoded contravariantly by the isomorphism class of the Sullivan minimal model. Isomorphic cohomology rings determine this type only when additional information, such as formality of a topological space, makes the cochain algebra equivalent to the cohomology algebra.

f:X→Y,g:Y→X

Homology obstruction to carrying surface curves onto one another

Words: 59
Homotopy equivalence OurBigBook.com
A homotopy equivalence of a closed surface cannot carry a simple closed curve of nonzero integral homology class onto a contractible simple closed curve. Any map into the latter factors through a circle whose inclusion induces zero on first homology; the former class would be killed by an isomorphism. Such a carrying map can nevertheless exist: project a handle generator onto a circle and compose with the contractible embedded circle.

Serre finiteness theorem for homotopy groups

Words: 80
Homotopy group OurBigBook.com
A simply connected CW complex of finite type has finitely generated homotopy groups in every degree. More generally, finite generation of its integral homology groups in each degree suffices. This is a finiteness theorem, not a claim that the groups are finite. A finite fundamental group allows the same conclusion after passing to a universal cover with finite type: a finite number of base cells lifts to a finite number of covering cells in each degree. It permits higher homotopy to be killed with finitely many cell attachments per dimension.

Principal bundles for a topological group give this construction through its classifying space. When C=K(A,n+1), the fibre is K(A,n) and the principal fibration is classified by Hn+1(B;A), yielding a principal Eilenberg–MacLane fibration.

A local trivialization makes F a retract of an open subset of Sm, so Hj(F;Q)=0 for j>m; the long exact sequence of homotopy groups of a fibration makes F connected. In the multiplicative rational Serre spectral sequence, only base columns zero and q occur. Since Hq(Sm)=0, a fibre class a∈Hq−1(F;Q) must satisfy dq​a=u, the base generator. Its degree is even. If as=0 is its first vanishing power, the derivation law gives 0=dq​(as)=suas−1=0 on the Eq​ page, a contradiction. Bounded fibre cohomology ensures such a vanishing power exists. In a homotopy of paths with endpoints fixed, a chosen lifted endpoint remains fixed because it varies continuously in a discrete fiber.

The nontrivial stabiliser subgroups are the conjugates of ⟨a⟩, ⟨b⟩ and ⟨ab⟩ at the three types of ramification points. Counting lifted cells gives the displayed Euler characteristic. A subgroup acts freely exactly when it meets every conjugate of these three cyclic groups trivially. Its quotient is then a regular covering of degree equal to the subgroup order, and quotient Euler characteristic is divided by that order.

Equality with the initial point would force t=0, where the rotation is nonzero; off the collars the original reflection already has no fixed points. Simplicial complex OurBigBook.com
A simplicial map sends vertices to vertices and sends the vertex set of every simplex to the vertex set of a simplex. It induces a continuous map between geometric realizations and a chain map between simplicial chain complexes.

Positive alternating simplex (+ei0​​,−ei1​​,…,(−1)keik​​,i0​<⋯<ik​)

Words: 126 Articles: 1
Simplicial map OurBigBook.com
For a simplicial map to the standard simplicial decomposition of a sphere, a k-simplex is positive alternating when its image has the displayed distinct labels. Reversing all signs makes it negative alternating. A collapsed or nonalternating simplex is neutral. Counting positive facets modulo two is the local ingredient in the antipodal alternating-simplex parity lemma.
Antipodal alternating-simplex parity lemma (pk​≡1(mod2))
Words: 81
Positive alternating simplex OurBigBook.com
An antipodal simplicial map from a regular antipodal triangulation of a sphere Sk to Fn has an odd number of positive alternating k-simplices. For each k-simplex, the number of positive alternating facets is odd exactly when the simplex is positive or negative alternating; otherwise it is even, including collapsed images. Count these incidences in one hemisphere: interior facets contribute twice, boundary facets once. Antipodal pairing then gives pk​≡pk−1​, starting with one positive vertex on S0. In particular, no such map exists when k>n.

Simplicial approximation theorem
Words: 91 Articles: 1
Simplicial approximation OurBigBook.com
For a finite simplicial complex K, a simplicial complex L, and a continuous map f:∣K∣→∣L∣, some iterated barycentric subdivision K(r) admits a simplicial approximation to f. The proof applies the Lebesgue number lemma to the inverse images of target open stars and uses that the mesh of a simplicial complex tends to zero under repeated barycentric subdivision.
Lower-dimensional sphere maps are null-homotopic
Words: 43
Simplicial approximation theorem OurBigBook.com
If n<m, every continuous map Sn→Sm is null-homotopic. After simplicial approximation, its image lies in the n-skeleton of a triangulation of Sm, hence omits a point. The punctured sphere is homeomorphic to Rm and is therefore contractible.

Manifold criterion for a suspension (SX is a manifold⟺X≅Sd)

Words: 114
Suspension (topology) OurBigBook.com
For a nonempty compact topological manifold Xd without boundary, its suspension is a topological manifold without boundary exactly when X is homeomorphic to Sd. The forward implication is a local homology from a link calculation at a suspension vertex: Hj​(X) is Z in degree d and zero elsewhere. For d≥2, put a coordinate ball between two nested cone neighbourhoods. The inclusion of their punctures is a homotopy equivalence but factors through the simply connected punctured ball, forcing π1​(X)=0. Thus X is a homotopy sphere, and the topological generalized Poincare theorem gives the result. The dimensions zero and one follow from the finite-set and circle classifications. Conversely S(Sd)≅Sd+1. If manifolds with boundary are allowed, the interval and its disk suspension show why this formulation needs the boundary restriction.

Complex projective space OurBigBook.com
The standard CW complex structure on Complex projective space has one cell in every even dimension from zero through 2n, and no odd-dimensional cells. Its cellular chain complex therefore has zero differential. The fundamental classes of the inclusions CPj↪CPn generate its even-degree integral homology; all other groups vanish.

Fixed-point property of even-dimensional complex projective space (L(f)=1+d+⋯+d2r=0)

Words: 117 Articles: 1
Complex projective space OurBigBook.com
Every continuous self-map of CP2r has a fixed point. If its pullback sends the integral degree-two generator to d times itself, multiplicativity gives trace dj in degree 2j. Thus its Lefschetz number is 1+d+⋯+d2r, which is positive: for d=1 it is (1−d2r+1)/(1−d)>0, and at d=1 it is 2r+1. The Lefschetz fixed-point theorem applies. In particular no nontrivial finite group acts freely on this simply connected space.

Complex projective plane has no nontrivial covering quotient

Words: 54
Fixed-point property of even-dimensional complex projective space OurBigBook.com
The Complex projective plane is simply connected. If it were the total space of a covering of degree at least two, it would be the universal cover and have a nonidentity deck transformation. Such a transformation acts by u↦±u on H∗(CP2)=Z[u]/(u3), giving Lefschetz number 1 or 3. It therefore has a fixed point, impossible for a nonidentity deck transformation.

Polynomial multiplication map to complex projective space ((CP1)m→CPm,(L1​,…,Lm​)↦∏i​Li​)

Words: 86
Complex projective space OurBigBook.com
Identify CPm with nonzero homogeneous binary forms of degree m, modulo nonzero scalar multiplication. Multiplication of m projective linear forms gives a well-defined holomorphic map: no product is zero, and scaling one form scales the entire coefficient vector. A form with m distinct roots has exactly m! ordered factorizations. In affine root coordinates the derivative is a Vandermonde determinant, nonzero at distinct roots. Each such preimage contributes +1 with complex orientations, so the mapping degree is m!. This also realizes the least positive degree allowed by the factorial degree obstruction for products of two-spheres.

The integral intersection form therefore has matrix (1), giving a unimodular intersection pairing. This computes a self-intersection through distinct representatives of the same class.

Let a,b≥2 with a+b=2n+1. Collapse the lower cells of Sa×Sb to obtain q:Sa×Sb→S2n+1 and compose with the Hopf fibration p:S2n+1→CPn. If the composite were nullhomotopic, homotopy lifting property would deform q into the circle fibre. Topological K-theory (K∗(X))

Words: 1k Articles: 39
Algebraic topology OurBigBook.com
Complex topological K-theory is the generalized cohomology theory built from stable equivalence classes of complex vector bundles. Its degree-zero group is the Grothendieck group K0(X), and its reduced theory is denoted K∗(X).

Odd topological K-theory (K1(X)=[X,UK​])

Words: 86
Topological K-theory OurBigBook.com
For compact metric X, odd topological K-theory is the homotopy set of norm-continuous maps into unitaries equal to the identity modulo compact operators on a fixed separable infinite-dimensional Hilbert space. Uniform finite-rank approximation over X and over homotopies gives the equivalent stable model colimN​[X,GLN​(C)]. Block sum gives an abelian group: a finite-dimensional unitary path swaps blocks, and a two-block rotation contracts diag(u,u−1) to the identity. On the circle the determinant winding identifies K1(S1) with Z; Bott periodicity gives K1(Sn)=Z in odd dimensions and zero in even dimensions.

Reidemeister torsion

Words: 60
Algebraic topology OurBigBook.com
For a based finite acyclic chain complex, Reidemeister torsion is an alternating product of determinants comparing each given chain basis with bases formed from boundaries and lifts of boundaries. With suitable local coefficients this gives an invariant of a space finer than its homology. Analytic torsion constructs a corresponding invariant from spectra of Laplacian operators, while Turaev torsion refines combinatorial sign and normalization choices.
